items.followUp: What is the role of chloroplasts in photosynthesis?

rubric.why: Identifies chromoplasts by their pigments and colour.
rubric.description: Defines chromoplasts as plastids containing coloured pigments.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying them as pigment-containing plastids that give colour to plant parts, especially flowers or fruits; accept either spelling of “colourful.”

rubric.why: Explains how flower colour helps pollination.
rubric.description: States that their colours attract pollinators.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking colourful flowers to attracting pollinators, such as insects.

modelAnswer: Chromoplasts are plastids that contain coloured pigments and give colour to flowers and fruits.
The bright colours of flowers attract pollinators, such as insects, and help in pollination.

items.followUp: Differentiate between a threatened species and an extinct species.

rubric.why: Shows that an extinct species has no living members remaining.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that no living members of the species remain anywhere.

rubric.why: Distinguishes endangered species as still existing but at risk.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the species still exists but is at risk of extinction.

modelAnswer: An extinct species has no living members remaining anywhere on Earth.
An endangered species still exists but is at risk of becoming extinct.

items.followUp: Write the taxonomic classification of a cat from kingdom to species.

rubric.why: Gives the first four taxonomic categories of human classification.
rubric.description: Names human kingdom, phylum, class and order.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct sequence: Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Mammalia, Order Primates.

rubric.why: Gives the final three taxonomic categories of human classification.
rubric.description: Names human family, genus and species.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct sequence: Family Hominidae, Genus Homo, Species sapiens.

modelAnswer: Kingdom: Animalia
Phylum: Chordata
Class: Mammalia
Order: Primates
Family: Hominidae
Genus: Homo
Species: sapiens

items.followUp: What is cytokinesis, and how does it occur in a plant cell?

rubric.why: Identifies the characteristic animal-cell method of cytokinesis.
rubric.description: Names the method as cleavage-furrow formation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that cytokinesis in an animal cell occurs by formation of a cleavage furrow.

rubric.why: Describes how the furrow divides the cell.
rubric.description: Explains the inward constriction that separates the daughter cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the cell membrane constricts inward until the cytoplasm is divided into two daughter cells.

modelAnswer: Cytokinesis in an animal cell occurs by the formation of a cleavage furrow.
The cell membrane constricts inward at the furrow until the cytoplasm separates into two daughter cells.

items.followUp: What may result when homologous chromosomes fail to separate during meiosis?

rubric.why: States the chromosome-separation failure that defines non-disjunction.
rubric.description: Defines non-disjunction as the failure of chromosomes or chromatids to separate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate during cell division.
Award 1 mark for stating that it produces cells or gametes with an abnormal number of chromosomes.

modelAnswer: Non-disjunction is the failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate during cell division.
It can produce daughter cells or gametes with an abnormal number of chromosomes.

items.followUp: Draw and label a diagram of metaphase II of meiosis.

rubric.why: Checks the defining arrangement of homologous chromosome pairs at metaphase I.
rubric.description: Shows homologous chromosome pairs aligned at the equator.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for drawing and labelling bivalents at the cell equator.

rubric.why: Checks that the diagram shows spindle attachment and essential labels.
rubric.description: Shows spindle fibres extending from opposite poles and labels key structures.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for showing spindle fibres attached to the chromosomes from opposite poles and including labels such as poles, spindle fibres and equator.

modelAnswer: Draw a cell outline as an oval 8 cm long and 5 cm wide.
Mark the two ends of the long axis as opposite poles; draw a 1 cm line through the centre to show the equator.
Draw two bivalents, each about 1 cm high, side by side on the equator; show each bivalent as two X-shaped homologous chromosomes.
Draw spindle fibres from each pole to the centromeres of the chromosomes, and label poles, spindle fibres, bivalents and equator.

items.followUp: How many ATP molecules are produced by aerobic and anaerobic respiration according to the textbook convention?

rubric.why: Gives the textbook yield for aerobic respiration.
rubric.description: States the ATP yield of aerobic respiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that aerobic respiration produces 38 ATP molecules.

rubric.why: Gives the textbook yield for anaerobic respiration.
rubric.description: States the ATP yield of anaerobic respiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that anaerobic respiration produces 2 ATP molecules.

modelAnswer: Aerobic respiration produces 38 ATP molecules.
Anaerobic respiration produces 2 ATP molecules.

items.followUp: Differentiate between reactants and products in a chemical reaction.

rubric.why: Identifies the substrate as the substance on which a reaction acts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a substrate is the substance on which an enzyme or reaction acts.

rubric.why: Identifies the product as what the reaction forms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a product is the substance formed as a result of a reaction.

modelAnswer: A substrate is the substance on which an enzyme or chemical reaction acts.
A product is the substance formed as a result of the reaction.
